Roofing Downtown's Innovation Quarter Labs and Historic Brick Stock

Downtown Winston-Salem's roof stock is unlike anywhere else in the market area: research labs and offices built into converted R.J. Reynolds tobacco factories in the Innovation Quarter, hotels occupying reworked historic towers, and older brick commercial buildings never designed for the rooftop loads modern tenants now put on them.

Lab and Life Science Roofs Inside Converted Tobacco Buildings

The Wake Forest Innovation Quarter's research and biotech tenants occupy buildings that started as tobacco manufacturing and warehouse space, with heavy timber or early steel structures never designed for the rooftop mechanical loads a modern lab requires. Fume exhaust, dedicated makeup air units, and redundant HVAC systems for climate-sensitive lab space add weight and penetration count the original structure has to be checked against before any new roof work goes on.

We start with a structural review on these conversions before specifying membrane, since a roof deck original to a decades-old tobacco warehouse may need reinforcement before it can carry current lab mechanical equipment, regardless of what membrane system gets chosen.

The Innovation Quarter's mix of restored brick manufacturing buildings and newer infill construction means no two roofs in the district follow the same rulebook. A building converted early in the district's development may have a different structural reinforcement approach than one converted more recently, and we confirm which approach was used before assuming a standard load capacity.

Historic Brick Parapets and Tobacco-Era Roof Details

Downtown's older brick buildings, many dating to the tobacco manufacturing era, carry parapet and coping conditions that differ significantly from a modern low-slope roof edge. Deteriorated mortar joints, aging coping stone, and old roof drain scuppers built into decorative brick detailing all need attention that a standard edge metal replacement wouldn't address on its own.

Water intrusion at these historic parapets often shows up as interior damage well below the roofline, since older brick assemblies can channel moisture down through the wall cavity rather than leaking straight through the deck. We treat parapet and coping condition as part of the roof scope on these buildings, not a separate masonry issue.

Hotel and Mixed-Use Roofs With Occupied Space Below

Hotels and mixed-use buildings downtown, some occupying towers built during the tobacco company's peak, run roofs above continuously occupied guest rooms and offices. Noise control, water intrusion prevention during active work, and coordination with building management for guest and tenant notice all shape how we sequence a project on these roofs differently than an unoccupied warehouse.

A tower roof also tends to have a smaller footprint but a taller, more complex parapet and setback profile than a low-slope warehouse, which changes the practical logistics of getting material and equipment to the roof level in the first place.

  • PVC or TPO systems specified after structural review on converted lab buildings
  • Historic parapet and coping repair alongside standard membrane work
  • Modified bitumen for lower-slope sections tying into original brick construction
  • Reinforced curb detailing for lab exhaust and makeup air penetrations
  • Noise and access sequencing for occupied hotel and mixed-use roofs

Code and Historic District Considerations

Some downtown buildings sit within a designated historic district, which can affect what's visible from the street level, including parapet caps, visible mechanical screening, and roof-mounted equipment. We confirm any relevant design review requirements before finalizing a scope on a building in that category.

That review can extend to material color and profile for anything visible from street level, so we confirm what's actually required before drafting a submittal package rather than assuming a standard commercial spec will pass without comment.

Documentation Standards for Institutional and Research Tenants

Research institutions and their landlords typically require a higher level of documentation than a standard commercial lease, since lab operations may need to certify roof and building envelope conditions as part of their own regulatory or accreditation requirements. We provide inspection and repair records formatted to support that kind of institutional review, going beyond a basic invoice and photo set.

For buildings with multiple lab tenants under one roof, we also track which rooftop equipment belongs to which tenant's lease, since makeup air units and exhaust systems installed at different times by different tenants can otherwise become a maintenance responsibility dispute.

What Downtown Building Managers Ask Us

Do converted tobacco warehouse buildings need extra structural review?

Yes. Original decks and framing weren't designed for modern lab mechanical loads, so we confirm structural capacity before specifying a membrane system on any Innovation Quarter conversion.

How do you handle roof leaks that show up as wall damage instead of ceiling damage?

On historic brick buildings, we check parapet and coping conditions first, since water often enters at the parapet and travels down through the wall cavity before showing up as interior damage well below the roofline.

Can roof work happen without disrupting a hotel's guests?

We sequence work to limit noise during guest hours where possible and coordinate directly with building management on notice and access, treating occupied guest space differently than we would an unoccupied building.

Does a building's historic district status affect roof work?

It can. Visible elements like parapet caps and rooftop equipment screening may fall under design review requirements, which we confirm before finalizing scope on any building in a designated historic district.

What roof systems work best above lab and research space?

The right system depends on the specific exhaust and makeup air configuration, but PVC and TPO are both common choices once structural capacity and penetration count are confirmed for the space below.
